title: Making a compost sieve from timber
subtitle: A simple riddle frame that separates fine finished compost from undecomposed material
excerpt: A compost sieve separates usable finished compost from twigs, half-decomposed material, and other debris that needs to go back into the heap. A simple version needs four pieces of timber, mesh hardware cloth, and an hour to assemble. It rests across a wheelbarrow and sieves compost in a single pass.
sourceNotes: Standard compost riddle construction guides from UK allotment and gardening organisations (RHS, National Allotment Society). Mesh specifications adapted from hardware cloth gauge standards.

glossaryTerms.definition: A coarse-mesh sieve used to separate fine compost from undecomposed larger particles. Also called a garden sieve or compost screen.

content.text: Compost heaps finish unevenly: fine soil-like material ready for use sits alongside undecomposed twigs and straw. A

extracts the usable material in a single step. The oversize material goes back into the heap for another cycle. A 10 mm mesh produces a fine compost suitable for seed sowing and potting mixes; 12 to 15 mm mesh gives a coarser material suitable for mulching and soil improvement.
4 pieces of 50 × 25 mm or 45 × 20 mm rough-sawn timber: two at 600 mm, two at 500 mm. (Offcuts from any project work.)
600 × 500 mm piece of galvanised hardware cloth (weld mesh), 10 mm or 12 mm aperture, from a garden centre or hardware store.
16 × 40 mm screws for the corner joints.
Galvanised staples or U-nails for fixing the mesh to the frame.

Butt-join the four pieces of timber into a rectangular frame: the two long (600 mm) pieces run along the outside edges; the two short (500 mm) pieces are sandwiched between them. Pre-drill and screw two screws per corner.
Lay the mesh over one face of the frame. Staple or U-nail at 50 mm intervals around the perimeter. Trim any protruding wire ends with wire cutters or pliers, or fold them over to prevent scratches.
No finish is required if using rough-sawn timber. If using PAR (planed), apply a coat of raw linseed oil to resist moisture.
Rest the sieve on the top edges of a wheelbarrow, mesh-side down. The frame sits within the barrow opening.
Lift a forkful of compost onto the sieve and shake with a circular motion. Fine material falls through into the barrow; large pieces remain on top.
Return the oversize material to the heap. Add some greens or a splash of water to the centre of the heap to restart breakdown.

rows.symptom: Compost is too wet and clogs the mesh
rows.cause: The compost was sieved too soon after a wet period or the heap had an excess of nitrogen-rich greens without enough browns
rows.fix: Spread the compost on a flat surface for a few hours in dry weather to lose surface moisture before sieving. If the heap is consistently wet, add shredded cardboard or straw to improve the C:N balance.
